models_evaluated: SAHIT neuroimaging model (logistic regression for functional outcome after aneurysmal SAH)

links.outcome: Between-site variation in c-statistic and calibration across 14 single-study external validations
links.effect: c-statistic ranged 0.52-0.84 (mean 0.74, I2=0.92); calibration intercept range -1.40 to 0.75 (I2=0.97); slope range 0.53-1.31 (I2=0.90).
links.quote: We observed a large variability in discriminative performance when evaluating the c -statistics at single-study external validation.

links.outcome: Case-mix and between-study heterogeneity as explanation of performance drop in validation cohorts
links.effect: Performance decline in 6 clusters attributable to case-mix variation, miscalibration, or both; e.g., IMASH Harrell's c 0.52 vs model-based 0.78; Leeds showed poor generalizability.
links.quote: We observed a substantial decrease in discriminative performance in 6 clusters compared to the optimism-corrected c -statistic (benchmark) and the pooled mean c-statistic (reference for overall external performance).

links.outcome: Whether single external validation cohort choice misrepresents model performance
links.effect: Validation in IMASH (0.52), Leeds (0.66), or ISAT (0.68) would suggest poor to moderate discrimination, while SHOP (0.84) was likely optimistic versus mean 0.74.
links.quote: For example, validating the model in the IMASH (0.52), Leeds (0.66), or the ISAT cluster (0.68) would indicate poor to moderate discrimination.

links.outcome: Need for local and continuous validation and updating given performance variability
links.effect: Authors state a single external validation cannot be decisive and local, continuous validation and updating are usually required; no temporal drift measured directly.
links.quote: We stress that a single single-study external validation cannot be interpreted as decisive proof of a well or poor model performance and that local and continuous validation is usually required.

unlisted_practices: Leave-one-cluster-out internal-external cross-validation on multi-cluster data instead of a single-study external validation
Membership model to quantify relatedness of derivation and validation cohorts (transportability)

links.effect: Mean c-statistic 0.74 (95%CI 0.70-0.78; range 0.52-0.84; I2=0.92); intercept and slope also had I2=0.97 and 0.90.
links.quote: The mean c-statistic was 0.74 (95%CI 0.70-0.78, range 0.52-0.84, I<sup>2</sup> = 0.92), the mean intercept was -0.06 (95%CI -0.37-0.24, range -1.40-0.75, I<sup>2</sup> = 0.97), and the mean slope was 0.96 (95%CI 0.78-1.13, range 0.53-1.31, I<sup>2</sup> = 0.90).

links.effect: Six clusters had substantial discrimination decreases versus optimism-corrected c-statistic 0.77 and pooled mean 0.75.
links.quote: We observed a substantial decrease in discriminative performance in 6 clusters compared to the optimism-corrected c -statistic (benchmark) and the pooled mean c-statistic (reference for overall external performance).

links.effect: Leeds, IMASH, Chicago declines attributed to case-mix: Harrell’s 0.66, 0.52, 0.76 versus model-based 0.76, 0.78, 0.73.
links.quote: Specifically, in the Leeds, IMASH, and Chicago clusters, this decline can be attributed to case-mix variation (Harrell’s 0.66, 0.52, and 0.76 versus model-based 0.76, 0.78, and 0.73, respectively).

links.effect: c-statistic variability largely due to between-study heterogeneity; I2=0.92.
links.quote: The I 2 -statistic was 0.92, indicating that the proportion of the total variability in the c -statistic was to a large extent explained by between-study heterogeneity.

links.effect: Leeds membership model c-statistic 0.69, but discrimination was unsatisfactory, indicating poor generalizability.
links.quote: In the Leeds cluster the derivation and validation samples were similar (membership model c -statistic 0.69), but the discriminative performance was unsatisfactory indicating poor generalizability of the model (Supplementary Material 7).

links.outcome: between-study heterogeneity in model discrimination across sites
links.effect: c-statistic varied from 0.52 to 0.84 across 14 external validation cohorts, with I2=0.92 showing variability was largely explained by between-study heterogeneity
links.quote: The I 2 -statistic was 0.92, indicating that the proportion of the total variability in the c -statistic was to a large extent explained by between-study heterogeneity.

links.outcome: performance drop in local cohorts versus development benchmark
links.effect: discriminative performance dropped substantially in 6 of 14 clusters compared to the optimism-corrected c-statistic benchmark of 0.77, reaching as low as 0.52
links.quote: We observed a substantial decrease in discriminative performance in 6 clusters compared to the optimism-corrected c -statistic (benchmark) and the pooled mean c-statistic (reference for overall external performance).

screen.practice: multi-cohort external validation before local implementation
screen.reason: The study empirically evaluates external validation methodology (single-study vs. cross-study meta-validation) for a clinical prediction model, demonstrating how single-study external validation can mislead implementation decisions.

primary.practice: multi-study validation versus single-study external validation
